The g-forces follow the envelope of the g-g diagram for a constant-radius turn (dashed line). The envelope of a motorcycle is not a circle: in such a turn the rear has to carry about half of the side force, and front braking unloads it. Wirtualny zawodnik i trener startują raz: The virtual rider and the coach start together from the gate. The rider follows the plan: throttle up to B, front brake from B, the bike starts leaning in at T, throttle at G. You can move point T nearer and farther, and wider and narrower. The coach rides the same bike, in the same body position and the same place on the seat, exactly as in the coach demo. The planner's rider is a simpler rider than the coach: it leans in and opens the throttle at the plan points and rides at the lean limit, while the coach keeps a margin. That is why, even with the coach's points, the rider can be faster or slower than the coach. The line comes out of the physics: from T the rider leans in as fast and as far as the bike and the speed allow, but so that the handlebar, the rear of the bike, the footpeg, the knee and the elbow clear the cone by the margin. The rider and the coach make no mistakes, so the same plan always gives the same result. Both brake while leaned over: leaning in, they ease off the front and the rear takes over the braking at once, hard at first, then less and less, and they hold it for a moment after getting on the gas. The braking force, the throttle roll-on and the cone margin are fixed for the bike, the body position and the seat position.

Wirtualny zawodnik: do H gaz, od H przed: The virtual rider: throttle up to B, then from B the front brake with the set force (full force after about 0.2 s), until T at the latest, down to the speed that fits the turn after T. At T the rider leans in by countersteering: for a fraction of a second the handlebar goes to the outside of the turn, the bike starts to roll, and only then does the handlebar turn in (thick on the lean trace of the chart; “countersteer” next to the steering angle in the “Now” table). At higher speed the roll starts faster. The same thing in reverse picks the bike up on exit: the handlebar turns further in. The rider also brakes while leaned over (trail braking): after T the front brake is released as the lean grows, because a leaned tyre has less grip left for braking, and as soon as the front is released the rear comes in: hard at first (up to about 80% of the grip the rear tyre has left at that lean), then less and less, until the bike has slowed to the apex speed or the rear has nothing left to brake with; then the throttle is cracked open and the rear is released only after about 0.2 s (overlap), so there is no moment without brake or throttle; the compressed fork shortens the trail, so the bike leans in faster. From T the rider leans in as fast and as far as the bike allows, but so that the outline (handlebar, rear of the bike, footpeg, knee and elbow) clears the cone by the margin, and rides at the lean limit (the coach in the demo keeps a margin). A late or narrow T means a tight turn right after T, so more braking is needed before it. Braking that starts too late cannot be made up while leaned over, and the bike runs wide. Then the rider holds the apex speed on a cracked throttle until G. From G the rider rolls on to full throttle, moves the body forward (the front wheel lifts later) and picks the bike up just enough for the tyres to carry the acceleration, so throttle at deeper lean means a wider exit. In the first loop (the right-hand one, straight after the start) the rider brakes and leans in like the coach, earlier than at B and T, because the speed out of the gate is higher and the approach comes from a different side; from the first left-hand loop on, braking starts at B. The gate 3 m behind the blue cone is an obstacle: a run in which the rider enters it does not count as finished. Leaning from upright to 45° takes about 0.35 s on the Ultra Bee, as in the video of a real run.
